title: [Rappler’s Best] ‘Be very, very afraid’
summary: This year's Social Good Summit brought together global, regional, and local perspectives on how AI has been both a boon and a bane to humanity — and what governance can do to stem a seeming point of…

blocks.text: We humans spent the last few days dissecting what’s been keeping us listless these days — artificial intelligence and the future of news.

Renowned historian and philosopher Yuval Harari warned us to be “very, very afraid” at this period in history. “AI is not a tool, it is an agent. It is something that can make decisions by itself. So it is taking power away from us,” he said.

But nothing is inevitable, Harari told Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa in a pre-recorded fireside chat that aired on Saturday, November 21, at Rappler’s annual Social Good Summit (SGS) at Shangri-La The Fort in Taguig. “There are still choices to be made.”

With the theme, “We, The Humans: Reclaim our Future,” this year’s SGS brought together global, regional, and local perspectives on how AI has been both a boon and a bane to humanity — and what governance can do to stem a seeming point of no return.

items: We’re in a “new imperial age,” Harari said, warning the Philippines that it risks losing control of critical infrastructure because of its dependence on foreign technology. Read more.

Staunch human rights advocate Agnès Callamard, secretary-general of Amnesty International, pushed for collective resistance to Big Tech’s unfettered and opaque inroads into our personal and professional lives. To do that and to fight back, humans must first understand AI, Ressa said.

Singaporean economist and AI executive Leslie Teo outlined ways to develop AI as a positive force for society. Read more. (We will be publishing more stories and videos from the summit in the coming days. Watch out for them.)

blocks.text: AI was also raised as a “growing concern” by the parliamentary body of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which held its 49th Summit in Manila last week. But whether the region intends to address it collectively is unclear.

In fact, the ASEAN Summit itself still failed to resolve critical regional issues that have been pending at the leaders’ desks: the civil war in Myanmar and the protracted negotiations for a South China Sea Code of Conduct. Read more.

In Turkey, the Antalya AI Pledge was launched on the sidelines of the COP 31 climate talks. It calls on governments and companies to take voluntary measures to power AI with cleaner energy. But China’s Alibaba is the only big tech company that has so far signed off on it.
Worse, the climate talks collapsed on Sunday, November 22, after leaders from the European Union and other countries rejected the final draft of a declaration that some deemed unambitious.

items: The draft acknowledged — for the first time — that global warming was on course to exceed the 1.5°C that countries had vowed to preserve. Read more.
The draft deal published on Thursday, November 19, removed any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels, prompting negotiators to extend their meetings to Sunday.
The first draft of the deal had already signaled tough negotiations ahead.

blocks.text: In Manila where realpolitik reigns, defense lawyers of Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial continued to mock the public with witnesses who are neither experts in their field, forthright in their answers, nor transparent in their practices. One was grilled over his “useless testimony.”

They got backups from ghosts — as the defense panel showed archived videos of the late senator Miriam Defensor Santiago and the late chief justice Renato Corona, who was convicted by the Senate impeachment court in 2013.

items: Huwag mong buhayin ang patay (Don’t resurrect the dead), wrote senior editor Herbie Gomez in his Pastilan piece.

Last week’s trial also miffed Thought Leader Chito de la Vega, who noted how he had been looking forward to what Duterte’s counsels boasted as a bombshell defense of their client. “Hanggang ngayon, nganga pa rin ako,” Chito wrote here. (I’m not sure that an English translation would do justice to that phrase.)
Former central bank deputy governor Diwa Guinigundo laments the lost opportunity to ferret out the truth about the allegations against the Vice President. Read more.
